mathgap.title: Signed Equality for Difference Statements
mathgap.principle: When a statement equates two differences, treat both sides as signed equations preserving the order of terms; do not take absolute values.
mathgap.when_to_apply: Whenever a sentence equates two differences, such as "the number of X that A has more than B equals the difference between C and D".
mathgap.example: Interpreting "A - B = C - D" as "|A - B| = |C - D|" or swapping the order to "B - A = D - C" leads to sign errors.

mathgap.title: Iterative Substitution and Propagation
mathgap.principle: Whenever a variable's value becomes known (through a direct count, a solved equation, or a transfer), immediately substitute that value into all other pending equations to propagate information.
mathgap.when_to_apply: After any step that yields a concrete numeric value for a person.
mathgap.example: Leaving an equation "X = Y + 5" unchanged after learning Y = 10, instead of substituting to get X = 15.

mathgap.title: Chronological Evaluation of Comparative Statements
mathgap.principle: Evaluate each comparative statement using the counts as they exist at that point in the text, after any earlier transfers or overrides have been applied.
mathgap.when_to_apply: When processing a comparative sentence, after all earlier transfers and direct‑count overrides affecting the involved persons have been applied.
mathgap.example: Using a person's original count in a comparison that appears after they have given away items.

mathgap.title: Query‑Focused Subsystem Extraction
mathgap.principle: Identify the minimal subset of equations that involve the queried person directly or indirectly, and solve only that subsystem, ignoring unrelated statements.
mathgap.when_to_apply: When the problem contains many statements and you need to focus on the queried variable.
mathgap.example: Attempting to solve the entire system including variables that never connect to the query, leading to unnecessary complexity.

mathgap.title: Distinct Name Disambiguation
mathgap.principle: Treat each unique name as a separate variable, even if names differ by only a single character; avoid conflating similarly spelled names.
mathgap.when_to_apply: Whenever a problem includes names that are similar but not identical (e.g., "Marlyn" vs "Marleen").
mathgap.example: Using the same variable for "Marlyn" and "Marleen" and merging their equations.

mathgap.title: Preserve Order in "Difference Between" Phrases
mathgap.principle: When a phrase says "the difference between the number of X that A and B have", interpret it as A - B, preserving the order as written.
mathgap.when_to_apply: Whenever a statement uses the wording "difference between ... A and B ...".
mathgap.example: Interpreting "difference between A and B" as B - A, swapping the intended order.

mathgap.title: General Comparative Interpretation (more/fewer)
mathgap.principle: Interpret "A has K more than B" as A - B = K, and "A has K fewer than B" as A - B = ‑K, preserving the direction of the comparison.
mathgap.when_to_apply: When a sentence directly states a numeric difference using "more" or "fewer".
mathgap.example: Reading "A has 5 more than B" as B - A = 5, reversing the subtraction order.

mathgap.title: Direct Count Handling with Overrides
mathgap.principle: When a statement says "X has N items", set X's count to N at that point, overriding any previous value for X.
mathgap.when_to_apply: Whenever a direct count appears, regardless of earlier information about that person.
mathgap.example: Keeping a previous count for X after encountering "X has 12" later in the text.

mathgap.title: Chronological Transfer Application
mathgap.principle: Apply each transfer statement in the order given, subtracting the specified amount from the giver and adding it to the receiver before processing any later statements.
mathgap.when_to_apply: When a sentence describes a transfer of items between two persons.
mathgap.example: Applying a later transfer before an earlier one, causing incorrect counts.

mathgap.title: Nested Difference Phrase Interpretation
mathgap.principle: When a statement uses a nested phrase like "the number of X that A has more than B" (or "has fewer than"), treat it as the signed difference A - B (or A - B = ‑K) and use it directly in equations, without assuming the difference is positive.
mathgap.when_to_apply: Whenever a comparative statement describes a difference using a nested phrase rather than a simple "has K more/fewer" clause.
mathgap.example: Treating "the number of oranges that Elisabeth has more than Dee" as |Elisabeth - Dee| instead of Elisabeth - Dee, leading to sign errors.

mathgap.description: Swapped direction in 'has K more than' statements
mathgap.why_it_happens: The model often reverses the subtraction order, interpreting "A has K more than B" as B - A = K.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Remember that "A has K more than B" translates to A - B = K; keep A on the left side of the subtraction.

mathgap.why_it_happens: The model assumes that any described difference must be non‑negative and thus takes the absolute value of the signed expression.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Keep the sign of the difference; use the signed expression directly (e.g., A - B = K) without applying absolute value.

mathgap.description: Ignoring the chronological order of transfers
mathgap.why_it_happens: The model updates counts after all transfers or applies them out of order, forgetting that later statements depend on earlier transfers.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Process transfers in the exact order they appear, updating giver and receiver before any subsequent statements.

mathgap.description: Treating 'has N' as an initial count regardless of position
mathgap.why_it_happens: The model treats every direct count as the starting value, even when it appears later and should override earlier values.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: When a direct count appears, set the variable to that number at that point, overriding any previous value.

mathgap.why_it_happens: The model sometimes reads phrases like "twice as many" as an addition rather than a multiplication.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Translate multiplicative language (e.g., "twice as many") into a multiplication equation (e.g., A = 2 * B).
